transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Nice to meet you too, Dr. Smith. Well, it’s a bit of a long story, but I guess... well, what brings me in is that I just feel like I’m always, always moving from one thing to the next. It’s like I can’t just idle, you know? Like a car that's just stuck in drive. 

I’ve been a customer service rep for years, mostly on the phones, and I usually found ways to deal with it on my own. In the old office, I'd pace around my cubicle, or fiddle with my headset, or just find excuses to walk over to the printer or the breakroom between calls. But they just completely overhauled our office—tore down the high walls, put us in this modern open-plan layout, new desk arrangements, the whole nine yards. And honestly, this new work setup has made it a lot harder to hide. 

Everyone can see everyone else now. My supervisor actually made a comment the other day about me being up and down like a yo-yo. It’s not like I’m trying to be disruptive or avoid my job, I just... I physically can't just sit there and do nothing when the phones are quiet. I have to be shifting, or standing, or moving to the next thing. And trying to force myself to just sit perfectly still and stare at a screen in this new desk all day is just completely exhausting me, so my wife finally told me I needed to come talk to someone about why I can't just relax and stay put.
Looking back at your childhood and school years, do you remember feeling this same need to be constantly moving or struggling to sit still in class?

Oh, gosh, looking back... yeah. Yeah, absolutely. I mean, this whole thing, it’s been around long, long before this recent job change. It’s funny you ask about school because my mother—bless her heart, she kept everything, every single report card in this big heavy green binder—and when my sister and I were cleaning out her house a few years ago, I actually sat down and looked through some of them. 

And it was just... well, it was exactly what you’re asking about. In grade school, pretty much every single teacher wrote the exact same thing in the comments section. They’d always start off nice, you know, they'd say, 'He’s a bright boy,' or 'He has a lot of potential,' but then right after that, there was always a 'but.' It was always, 'but he’s careless with his assignments.' Or they’d write that I talked out of turn. I was a real chatterbox, I guess, just blurting things out when I was supposed to be listening to the lesson. 

And they constantly—I mean, constantly—had to remind me to just stay with my work. I’d be doing a math worksheet and then suddenly I’m looking out the window at the playground, or I'm tapping my pencil into a rhythm, or trying to talk to the kid next to me about whatever television show was on the night before. I just couldn't lock in on one thing if it wasn't moving fast enough for me. I actually remember Mrs. Gable in fourth grade, she moved my desk right up next to hers at the front of the room just so she could reach over and tap my paper every five minutes to keep me on track. It was pretty embarrassing, really, having all the other kids looking at you like that, but I just... I couldn't help it. I'd try to sit still, I really would, but the energy just had to go somewhere. So, yeah, I guess to make a long story short, it's definitely not a new thing at all.
